en: Let's leave the stack, which was a great
data structure,
and let's move on to the queue.
Now what's a queue?
Just like a stack, a queue could be
described as a simplified array. So it's
also still a list structure. It's for
managing values, not key values, just
values.
And the difference to the normal array, but
also the difference to the stack, is that in
a queue we have some items,
but then we can enqueue
a new item, which basically means we add
this item at the beginning of the list,
and we can dequeue our item from the end of
the list. So for the stack, we could always
add items at the end and remove them from
there, or do the same at the beginning,
but we always worked on the same end of of
the list for the stack. Now for the queue,
we work on both ends of the list and we add
new items always at the beginning
and we remove items always at the end.
Of course you could switch this, but the key
thing that makes up a queue is simply that
you always work on different ends. You never
remove on the end where you added. You
always do that on the other end.
And therefore a queue is a FIFO. Structure.
It's a first-in-first-out structure because
the item we removed here
by dequeuing it was the item that originally
was added to the list first.
The item on the left, 1.19, is the item we
added last and it will be the last item to
be removed because a queue is FIFO,
first-in-first-out.
Now just as before, it might be easier to
grasp the idea of a queue if we consider
some real-world examples.
And for queues, we got a lot of examples.
Actually, in the real world, we also know
queues.
If you're waiting for something in the post
office
because you need to hand in a letter there,
or if you're on the supermarket and you need
to pay and you're waiting until it's your
turn,
you're in a queue.
You were added to the queue last
and the first item to be processed is the
person who
was added to the queue first. So the first
person that waited to pay or whatever queue
you're in.
That's a queue. We have it in real life all
the time. It's the default way of waiting
for something. It's always such that the
first person is
the first one to act and the last person to
wait for something is the last one to act
and that's a queue.
And of course, we therefore can also use
queues in programming. For example, if
you're building a chat application
and those chat messages are sent to a server
and should then be sent forward to the other
chat partner, the other participant in the
chat, they should of course be delivered in
order. So the first message sent by the
sender should be the first message received
by the other chat partner. And the last
message sent should be the last message
received. So queues are everywhere and hence
sometimes we want data structures that are
really limited to these 2 operations,
enqueueing and dequeuing.
